what: Frontdoor sells home service plans. A homeowner pays a monthly fee, and when the air conditioning, boiler, dishwasher or plumbing breaks, Frontdoor sends a contractor and covers the repair. Its main brand is American Home Shield, and it has added on-demand repair services and a cheaper plan called Frontdoor.
customers: American homeowners, often buying the plan when they purchase a house through a real estate agent, and increasingly directly online. The contractors who do the work are an independent network rather than employees.
money: Existing customers renewing their home service plan, the most profitable revenue.
New customers, sold through real estate agents and direct channels.
On-demand repairs, parts and related services.
moat: This is an insurance business wearing a home services label, and the economics follow: it collects premiums monthly and pays claims when something breaks, so the skill is pricing the risk and controlling the cost per claim. The contractor network, built over decades, is the hard part to copy — it is what lets Frontdoor get someone to a house quickly at a negotiated price, which neither a new entrant nor a homeowner calling around can match.
risks: Growth depends on new customers, and the traditional channel — plans sold when a house changes hands — has been weak because fewer houses are being sold.
Cost per claim rises with contractor labour and parts inflation, and the plan price can only be raised at renewal, so margins compress when inflation runs ahead.
The shares trade at about 22.4 times earnings and 12.5 times EV/EBITDA.
Debt of $1.2B is partly offset by $566.0M of cash, but it was taken on for an acquisition that has to earn its cost.
Only five analysts cover the stock, so the $104.60 average target rests on few opinions.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $1.6B in 2021 to $2.1B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $2.2B.
Renewals are roughly three-quarters of revenue, recurring and far more profitable than first-year plans.
Free cash flow of $393.0M against a $6.1B market value is strong, and the business needs little capital.
American housing stock is old and appliances are expensive to replace, which is the structural reason the product exists.
A recovery in home sales would restart the real estate agent channel, which is currently the weakest part of the funnel.
watch: Net customer additions and the cost per claim. One shows whether the funnel is working while home sales are weak; the other shows whether the pricing is keeping up with repair costs.
view: The useful way to look at Frontdoor is to stop thinking of it as a home services company and start thinking of it as a small insurer. It collects a monthly premium, promises to pay when a specified thing breaks, and makes money on the difference between premiums and claims. Everything that matters follows from that framing: the skill is actuarial pricing and claims cost control, and the moat is the contractor network that lets it settle a claim cheaply and fast.

That network is genuinely hard to replicate and it is underrated as an asset. When a homeowner’s air conditioning fails in August, the value Frontdoor delivers is not the money — it is that someone competent arrives tomorrow at a price already negotiated. Building the relationships to do that across the United States took decades, and it is why a well-funded newcomer cannot simply buy its way in. It also means claims cost less for Frontdoor than the same repair would cost the homeowner, which is where the margin comes from.

The weakness is the top of the funnel. A large share of new customers has historically come through real estate agents when a house changes hands, and houses have not been changing hands. That is why the company has pushed direct-to-consumer sales and a cheaper plan — sensible moves, and they are working well enough to keep revenue growing from $1.6 billion to $2.1 billion through the worst housing market in decades. But it means a chunk of the growth is currently being bought with marketing rather than arriving free with a house sale.

At 22.4 times earnings with $393 million of free cash flow, this is a fair price for a decent recurring-revenue business with a genuine moat and a cyclical headwind that will eventually reverse. The thing that would change my view in either direction is the cost per claim: if contractor labour and parts inflation keeps outrunning what Frontdoor can charge at renewal, the insurance maths deteriorates quietly and the margin goes with it. That number matters more here than revenue growth, and it gets far less attention.
bull: Home sales recover and restart the agent channel on top of a direct business that already works, while renewals keep compounding at high margin.
bear: Repair cost inflation outruns what can be charged at renewal, the claims margin erodes, and customer growth stays dependent on paid marketing.
